title: Address to State Lookup: Census-Verified State
description: Verify an address's state against Census polygons with Address to State Lookup — state FIPS, highlighted boundary and context. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, an address in Kansas City can sit in Missouri or Kansas — the polygon knows which, even when the mailing address is coy about it.
quick_answer: Address to State Lookup verifies which US state an address, place or point falls in by testing it against Census Bureau state polygons, and returns the state FIPS code with a highlighted boundary and demographic context. Read a state answer that comes from geography, not from parsing text.
steps_intro: Mostly state is obvious — until a border city, a mailing address or a data error makes it a question. Answer it geographically:

body.t: Kansas City, Texarkana, Bristol, the Quad Cities: mailing labels blur state lines that polygons do not. Verify the side that matters.
State-level obligations follow the physical state. A verified point-in-polygon answer beats a parsed string in any audit.
State fields cleaned by geography stop the errors that text-parsing imports. The county sibling adds the finer grain:
“Which state is this actually in?” — for exclaves, river bends and changed channels, the polygon has opinions worth hearing.
Kansas City exists in both Kansas and Missouri, divided by a state line the river drew. The lookup tests the point — the only honest way to answer for a specific address.
Texas is FIPS 48, New York 36, California 06 — the code beside the name is what lets two databases confirm they mean the same state.

faq: Can I search a full street address?
Yes — address, city, ZIP or coordinates all resolve to a point, and the point is tested against the state polygon.
Does it return the state FIPS code?
Yes, alongside the highlighted boundary — the two-digit code that databases use to agree about states.
Are demographics current live counts?
No — they are Census survey estimates (ACS) with a stated vintage. Nobody counts a state's population live; honest tools say so.
Can I click the map instead of searching?
Yes — clicking drops the point and the same polygon test runs. Useful for fields, parcels and middle-of-nowhere questions.
Does it work outside the United States?
The polygon framework is US Census geography. Outside the US, the country and continent tools elsewhere on the site take over.
Why not just read the state from the address?
Because addresses carry mailing cities across state lines and data entry makes typos. The point-in-polygon test is immune to both.
What about territories?
Census geography covers the territories with their own FIPS codes; the lookup follows the framework it is built on.
A river moved — which state now?
State boundaries often follow the historical channel, not today's water. The polygon holds the legal line, which is exactly why the test is worth running.
Can a ZIP code span two states?
ZIPs serve delivery routes and can cross lines the polygons respect. Another reason the point, not the postcode, is tested.
The point is on a military base or reservation.
The state answer still applies geographically; jurisdiction layers (federal, tribal) sit on top and are separate questions the demographics frame but do not settle.
How current is the boundary?
Census geography is refreshed on the Bureau's cycle; annexations and rare boundary compacts land there first among public sources.
